'''''Ceiba chodatii''''', the '''floss silk tree''', is a species of [[deciduous]] [[tree]] native to the [[tropical]] and [[subtropical]] forests of [[South America]]. It has a bottle-shaped swollen trunk in which water is stored for the dry season and is known locally as '''palo borracho'''.

==Description==
[[File:Ceiba chodatii flowers.jpg|thumb|left|Flowers of ''Ceiba chodatii'']]
''Ceiba chodatii'' is a medium-sized deciduous tree with a tall, stout, bare trunk. It grows to about {{convert|12|m}} tall, has a number of thick branches at the top of the swollen trunk and has a rounded crown. The bark is smooth with vertical ridges and horizontal wrinkles. It contains [[chlorophyll]] and is green when young and able to [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesize]], but turns grey with age. It is covered with thick, woody conical spines. The alternate leaves are palmate with five lobes and serrated edges. The flowers are large, solitary and creamy white with a few purple flecks. They are up to {{convert|15|cm}} long with yellow-green [[Sepal|calyces]] and funnel-shaped [[Petal|corollas]] with five fleshy, hairy petals joined at the base. The fruit is a large, oblong green capsule. When ripe it splits open to reveal black seeds surrounded by a mass of white fibres resembling cotton.<ref name=Gibbs>{{cite web |url=https://www.academia.edu/2565941/A_TAXONOMIC_REVISION_OF_THE_GENUS_CEIBA_MILL._BOMBACACEAE_ |title=A taxonomic revision of the genus ''Ceiba'' Mill. (Bombacaceae) |author1=Gibbs, P. E. |author2=Semir, J. Año |year=2003 | issn = 0211-1322 |accessdate=2013-06-22}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Ceiba chodatii'' is native to the forests of Bolivia, the [[Chaco (Paraguay)|Chaco]] region of Paraguay and the Piedmont Mountains of western Argentina where it is found in seasonally dry woodlands. It flowers between February and May.<ref name=Gibbs/>

==Ecology==
The flowers open at dusk and are probably pollinated by [[Sphingidae|sphingid moths]]. Other members of the genus are pollinated by [[bat]]s but this seems unlikely for ''Ceiba chodatii'' as the flowers produce little nectar. [[Hummingbird]]s also visit the flowers but do not touch the anthers or stigma. Self-pollination does not occur in this species because of a late-acting form of [[Self-incompatibility in plants|self-incompatibility]].<ref name=Gibbs/>

The bottle-shaped trunk is swollen with water being retained by the tree for use in the dry season.<ref name=NHM/> The indigenous people of the Chaco make use of this water for their cattle and the timber is used to make [[canoe]]s and articles for daily use. Fibres from the trunk are woven into ropes and extracts from the bark are used for tanning and as a dye.<ref name=NHM>{{cite web |url=http://www.nhm.ac.uk/nature-online/species-of-the-day/biodiversity/economic-impact/ceiba-chodatii/ |title=''Ceiba chodatii'' (palo borracho, palo botella, samu’u) |author=Chocarro, Maria Peña |publisher=Natural History Museum |accessdate=2013-06-23}}</ref>

The dry chaco where this tree is found has dense spiny woodlands consisting of low trees and an understorey of [[Aspidosperma]], [[Astronium]], [[Schinopsis]], Ceiba, and [[Bulnesia]]. The ground is clad in thorny plants, some with [[microphyll]]s and others with no leaves and cacti such as ''[[Cereus (plant)|Cereus]]'' and ''[[Stetsonia (plant)|Stetsonia]]''. Some plants such as ''[[Jacaratia]]'' accumulate water in tubercles.<ref name=NHM/>
